description: CeJN's internal search syntax, CPV taxonomy, notice URL pattern and pagination are unknown because the portal is JS-rendered and was not opened with a browser in this pass.

Simple procurements (goods/services up to EUR 15,000; works up to EUR 30,000) bypass full CeJN procedures and appear only in contracting authorities' semi-annual reports - exactly the size band of many POS terminal, terminal-maintenance and small kiosk orders.

Several likely payments-adjacent contracting authorities were reasoned about but not individually verified this pass: Fond za zdravstveno osiguranje, Fond PIO, Ministarstvo finansija/Državni trezor, Uprava za katastar, EPCG, Crnogorski elektrodistributivni sistem, Aerodromi Crne Gore, Luka Bar.
Službeni list Crne Gore (official gazette) was not directly located or profiled, although it is the authoritative publication venue for the procurement law and its sub-regulations.

Coverage of award notices ('obavještenje o ishodu postupka') and signed contracts/annexes was only indirectly evidenced (a single CBCG award PDF mirrored on nabavke.com); the CeJN contract register was not located.
No confirmed English-language interface for CeJN was found; UJN offers /en/ pages but the notice content itself is Montenegrin only.

The internal structure of CEJN — the URL scheme, filter parameters and any JSON/API endpoints for its plan, decision and contract modules — was not established, because the site is client-rendered and no documentation surfaced.

No CPV code shortlist for banking and payments (ATM/POS terminals, card personalisation, cash-handling equipment, payment processing services, core banking software) was assembled for filtering Montenegrin and TED award records.

The set of Montenegrin contracting authorities that actually buy banking/payments technology was only partially identified (CBCG confirmed; Skupština, DRI, Monstat, Komunalne usluge Podgorica found as pattern examples). Uprava prihoda i carina, Ministarstvo finansija, Pošta Crne Gore, Investiciono-razvojni fond / Razvojna banka Crne Gore, Fond PIO, Fond zdravstva and the municipalities were not confirmed to have retrievable plan/contract pages.
No route was established for retrieving award decisions and contracts from before the current CEJN generation, nor for the pre-2019-law era under the old Uprava za javne nabavke portal.
All local-language querying was done in Latin-script ijekavian Serbian. Cyrillic variants and Montenegrin-specific letters (ś, ź) were not tested, nor were transliterations of vendor names.

CEJN is described as covering contract execution reports (izvještaji o izvršenju ugovora) and Institut alternativa flags contract amendments (aneksi ugovora) as under-reported, but no actual annex or execution-report artefact was located in this pass.
Whether nabavke.com's award documents and detail pages are fully open or partly subscription-gated, and what its terms of service say about automated collection, was not determined.
No confirmed public list of fiscalisation-approved POS/ENU device and software vendors was located, so the terminal supply chain remains unenumerated at the authoritative level.

The roster of contracting authorities (naručioci) — public and sectoral — was not extracted; only the legal definition and the registration mechanism were confirmed. Municipalities and state-owned enterprises (Pošta CG, utilities) are likely a large share of POS-adjacent demand.

Insurance supervision (Agencija za nadzor osiguranja) and microcredit/leasing institution registers were referenced conceptually via CBCG's financial-system pages but no specific register URL was confirmed for the insurance supervisor.
None of the identified registers were confirmed to offer an API, bulk export or open-data dump; all appear to be HTML pages or form-driven search.
EU-level pointer assets that would list Montenegrin buyers and awards (TED, EU IPA-funded contract award databases, EBRD/World Bank procurement notice archives) were not covered in this cell.

Pricing, licensing terms and redistribution rights for every commercial aggregator in this cell (eTenderi.me, TenderiLIVE, eKapija Tenderi, javne-nabavke.com, MontenegroTenders, TendersOnTime, TendersInfo, GlobalTenders, DevelopmentAid) are unknown; none were verified against their ToS.

It is unknown how much each aggregator adds over the official CeJN portal, or how much the aggregators duplicate one another — especially the global family (MontenegroTenders, TendersOnTime, TendersInfo, GlobalTenders) which may all resell the same harvest.
Private-sector RFPs from Montenegrin commercial banks and payment institutions are largely uncovered; only eKapija claims commercial-company tenders, and that claim is unverified for ME specifically.
Archive depth — how far back each aggregator retains notices the original publisher has deleted — was not established for any source in this cell.

Local-language (sr/cnr) discovery surfaced ME-focused services well, but no Albanian-language channel was checked despite a significant Albanian-speaking minority and cross-border AL/XK vendor activity.
Only one fetch was attempted in this cell and it failed at the transport layer; all other URLs come from search-result metadata and have not been retrieved.
Internal audit function (interna revizija) inside ministries, state funds and the central bank, and the Ministry of Finance's central harmonisation unit for internal audit, were not covered.
Parliamentary oversight of audit findings (Skupština Crne Gore, Odbor za ekonomiju, finansije i budžet; Odbor za antikorupciju) not explored — search budget ran out.
No auditor/watchdog output located that names IT or payment-services suppliers to Montenegrin public banks/financial institutions, which is the commercial core of the run scope.
Montenegrin-Cyrillic and alternative orthography variants (e.g. 'јавне набавке', 'ревизија') were not used as search variants; only Latin-script Montenegrin/Serbian and English were searched.
No check was made for RSS feeds, sitemaps, or open-data/API endpoints on dri.co.me, institut-alternativa.org, antikorupcija.me, so collection method recommendations are crawl-based assumptions.

Transparency International's regional/national presence, the EU Commission's annual Montenegro country report (Chapter 5 – public procurement), and the EU Delegation's monitoring were not separately profiled.

No regional ICT/fintech trade press assessed (Netokracija, ICTbusiness.info, Fintech Serbia/Balkans, Kapital.hr tech desks) — the channel most likely to name core-banking, card-processing and ATM/POS vendors winning Montenegrin bank deals.
No enumeration of Montenegrin commercial banks' own newsrooms/press sections, which typically publish signing announcements and vendor partnerships that media then pick up.
Only Latin-script Montenegrin/Serbian terms were used. Dan publishes under a Cyrillic masthead (ДАН appeared in results), and Cyrillic-script queries were never run.
Search surfaced mostly current-year items; no assessment of archive depth, paywall history or availability of past-year procurement affairs in any outlet.

CIN-CG (Centar za istraživačko novinarstvo Crne Gore) was queried but search resolved to the Bosnian CIN instead; the Montenegrin investigative centre's own domain was never returned, so it is not listed as a candidate.
Several listed pointers (eKapija, Tenderi Live, javne-nabavke.com, SeeNews, Bloomberg Adria) are paywalled or subscription-gated, so unlicensed automated collection is not appropriate.

Global hardware/software vendor partner-locator pages filtered to Montenegro (Ingenico, PAX, Verifone, Diebold Nixdorf, NCR Atleos, Hyosung, Temenos, Oracle FS, Finastra, BPC, OpenWay, Halcom, Comtrade, S&T/Kontron) were not enumerated.
Non-bank PSPs, e-money institutions and payment institutions licensed by CBCG were not separately enumerated; hiring and partner signals from that segment are uncovered.
No searching was done in Montenegrin Cyrillic script or with Albanian-language terms (used by part of the Montenegrin population and by regional integrators operating from Kosovo/Albania).
Job ads and event sponsor pages are highly perishable — ads expire in weeks and sponsor logo walls are replaced each edition — yet no archival strategy is established.

Bank annual reports published on the banks' own investor-relations pages (as opposed to CBCG/SCMN copies) were not individually located; these often carry richer narrative on digitalisation programmes.

Službeni list Crne Gore (official gazette) is not documented as a monitored source, despite being the only legally definitive publication venue for the Law on Public Procurement, its amendments and every bylaw.

No state audit institution (Državna revizorska institucija) or budget-inspection source captured. Montenegro's Chapter 5 commitments explicitly include strengthened budget-inspection controls, so audit reports will be the main evidence of contracts awarded outside published procedures.

The European Commission's own Montenegro enlargement/progress report and the EU Council common position on Chapter 5 were referenced only second-hand through eu.me and national press; the primary EU documents are not registered.

Reporting flagged a March 2025 Montenegro-UAE intergovernmental cooperation agreement that exempts certain contracts from procurement procedures. Contracts under such bilateral instruments never reach CEJN and are invisible to every notice-scanning cell.

Only one domestic Montenegrin law firm was identified with a procurement angle, and no regional firm (Karanović, BDK, Harrisons, Moravcevic Vojnovic, Prelević) was verified as publishing ME procurement commentary.

The Q2 2026 commitments (amended Law on Public Procurement, amended anti-corruption law, red-flag module in the e-procurement system) have no single tracked document trail; they are currently known only through news and eu.me summaries.
The Commission decision database's underlying query mechanics (URL parameters, pagination, whether decision PDFs are directly addressable) were not reverse-engineered.

Parliamentary oversight of procurement bodies (Skupština Crne Gore — Odbor za ekonomiju, finansije i budžet, and Odbor za antikorupciju) was not directly searched; committee hearings and adopted reports on the Commission and DRI are a likely source of aggregate data and political signals.

Agencija za sprječavanje korupcije (ASK) and Uprava za inspekcijske poslove were not covered; ASK handles conflict-of-interest and integrity plans in procurement, and inspection bodies conduct procurement-compliance supervision.
Službeni list Crne Gore (official gazette) was not indexed as a source for procurement-law amendments and bylaws establishing thresholds and appeal fees.

Coverage relied on Montenegrin/Serbian latinica. Cyrillic-script variants and Montenegrin-specific orthography (izvještaj vs izveštaj, rješenje vs rešenje) were not systematically exercised, and no Albanian-language search was run despite a significant Albanian-speaking minority.
EU-level and regional aggregators that mirror Montenegrin notices — TED, Balkan Tender Watch's regional database, and Open Contracting Data Standard mirrors — were not investigated for ME coverage.

Sector buyers not yet mapped to a procurement URL: CGES (transmission), Željeznička infrastruktura CG and Željeznički prevoz CG (rail), Montecargo, Barska plovidba, Regionalni vodovod Crnogorsko primorje, Zavod za zapošljavanje, plus the ~20 municipal ViK and Čistoća utilities outside Podgorica and Bar.

The authoritative central portal (CeJN) is a JavaScript SPA and was not readable by plain fetch. Whether it exposes contracting-authority filtering, CPV codes, award values, bulk export or an RSS/JSON API is unknown.

Coverage of sr-Cyrl (Cyrillic) renderings is untested. FZOCG serves pages in both Latin and Cyrillic script, and other public funds may too; a Latin-only crawler could silently miss or duplicate content.

Award notices and contract values are under-covered relative to calls for tender. Only fragmentary award data was found (CEDIS meter tender values and bidder counts came from trade press, not a primary award feed; the Monteput toll award likewise).

Historical depth is unclear for every SOE page examined. Pošta's page showed only 2020 items; Luka Bar's category paginates but the depth of the archive was not probed; no site was confirmed to retain multi-year notice history.

Indirect/revealing sources are thin for this cell — SOE annual reports, board (upravni odbor) minutes, state-audit reports (Državna revizorska institucija) on SOEs, and the funds' 'analitičke kartice' spend ledgers were noted but not systematically sourced.
CEJN (cejn.gov.me) could not be read without JavaScript, so CBCG's national-portal procurement record — plans, tender documentation, award-outcome notices — remains unmapped.
CBCG's annual procurement plan (plan javnih nabavki) and any contract register were not located in any public location.

How the RTS/X payment system and the TIPS Clone platform were actually contracted is unresolved. The TIPS Clone is World Bank financed (EUR 8m) and technically supplied via Banca d'Italia under Eurosystem auspices, which may mean much of it never passes through a competitive tender at all.
Službeni list Crne Gore (Official Gazette) was not queried in this pass. CBCG decisions, operating rules for the payment system, and international cooperation agreements are promulgated there.

Vendor-side sources were not scouted: banknote/coin processing and authentication suppliers (e.g. Giesecke+Devrient, Koenig & Bauer Banknote Solutions, Toshiba, Glory, CPS/cash-cycle integrators) and payments-platform integrators publish customer references, press releases and case studies that reveal CBCG contracts after award.

Searching was done in Montenegrin/Serbian Latin script only. Cyrillic-script variants ('Централна банка Црне Горе', 'јавне набавке') and Italian-language sources (Banca d'Italia's own TIPS Clone communications and procurement) were not queried.
Historical depth is thin. The CBCG tender page shows a sparse and uneven archive (2026, 2025, 2023, 2019, 2018) with apparent gaps, and no archived snapshots were checked.

Council of Europe Development Bank (CEB), IFC, and bilateral donors beyond KfW (e.g. Austrian ADA, Italian Cooperation, USAID successors, Swiss SECO) were not systematically checked for Montenegro financial-sector tenders.
The procurement plan for the World Bank SEPA/TIPS-clone project (indicative contract packages, methods, timing) was not extracted; only the PAD was located.
ECEPP and UNGM lack confirmed, ToU-compliant bulk/API access paths; only per-notice URLs were observed.

The Montenegrin-language vocabulary for donor tenders was only partially harvested (EU tenderi, poziv za dostavljanje ponuda, obavještenje o ugovoru, ugovaranje, IPA, digitalizacija plaćanja); no controlled glossary with transliterations and noisy-term flags was produced.
Historical award archives (who won past donor-funded Montenegro financial/IT contracts) were only touched via Finances One; TED and ECEPP award histories were not mined.

Official domains for Universal Capital Bank, Adriatic Bank, Lovćen banka, Addiko Podgorica and Razvojna banka/IRF were inferred from branding rather than confirmed from an authoritative register during this run.
CKB banka, the market leader and the most important private buyer in the cell, was never successfully read because of a TLS chain failure.

Searching was carried out in Serbian/Montenegrin and English as required, but no searching was done in Turkish (for Ziraat's parent-group announcements), Slovenian (for NLB Group sourcing), German (Erste Group) or Hungarian (OTP Group, CKB's owner). Group-level procurement for four of the largest ME banks is likely documented only in the parent's language.

No supplier-side registry or contract-registry route was explored for Montenegro: the Central Registry of Business Entities (CRPS), court/insolvency filings, and bank annual-report notes on outsourcing and related-party supplier transactions were not searched in this run.

Bank social and recruitment channels were not searched. LinkedIn job posts for procurement/vendor-management roles, and bank LinkedIn/Facebook posts announcing technology partners, are a common leak route in small markets. Hipotekarna banka's active Facebook presence was observed but not mined.
Of the candidates listed, only nlb.me, hipotekarnabanka.com and erstebank.me were actually fetched. All other URLs come from search-result metadata or reasoned inference and carry no liveness claim.

ZIRAAT Bank Montenegro AD Podgorica's own website could not be identified in this pass (only SWIFT directories, thebanks.eu, the Montenegrin securities-market entry at scmn.me and a directory listing at Bulevar Ivana Crnojevića 101, Podgorica). Without the domain, the hypothesised /ihaleler-style subsidiary tender page cannot be probed.

The vendor side was not systematically scouted. Payments and banking-technology suppliers (processors, card personalisation bureaux, ATM/self-service, core banking) routinely publish 'selected by <Group> across N markets' press releases naming Montenegro, which is frequently the only public trace of a group framework agreement.

EU/EBRD/IFC and other IFI procurement-notice channels were not searched. Where a parent group runs a donor- or IFI-financed programme (digitalisation, green lending platforms) that touches the Montenegrin subsidiary, procurement is competed under IFI rules and published — a genuinely public tender feed in a cell that otherwise has none.

The two most operationally valuable channels (the OTP SAP Ariba buyer instance and any Erste equivalent) are invitation-gated. Automated collection is impossible and probably impermissible; there is no public projection of their event calendars.

Erste Group Procurement's e-sourcing platform was not identified. Searches did not establish whether EGP runs SAP Ariba, Jaggaer, Coupa or an in-house tool, so the registration path for the largest centrally-managed spend pool in this cell is unknown.

No German-language parent-procurement glossary was built for Erste and Addiko beyond incidental terms observed on the EGP page (Lieferantenmanagement, Beschaffung, Tochtergesellschaften). Ausschreibung, Vergabe, Rahmenvereinbarung, Lieferantenportal and Einkauf were not systematically searched.

The DORA Register-of-Information regime covers EU-supervised entities, so it captures Erste, NLB and Addiko group vendor inventories but not OTP's Montenegrin subsidiary, and Montenegro itself is outside the EU supervisory perimeter. The CBCG's own outsourcing/ICT-third-party notification requirements were not investigated.
Card personalisation and card switch/processing suppliers to Montenegrin banks were not identified from the supplier side in this pass.
No per-bank vendor attribution table exists yet for the ~11-15 licensed Montenegrin banks.
Local vendor primary websites (Logate, ČIKOM, Amplitudo, Printec Montenegro) were identified but their reference/news pages were not directly retrieved, so their customer lists are unread.
LinkedIn is repeatedly the richest supplier-announcement channel for this market but is platform-gated and was only sampled indirectly.
Vendor claims are unverified against buyer-side award records (complementary cells 7-8).
Cash-in-transit, cash-centre and ATM cash-management operators in Montenegro are entirely unmapped, as is the licensing register for private security agencies that would list them.

The card-processing layer for Montenegro was not resolved: it is unclear which processors (in-house bank platforms, regional processors, or group processors of foreign bank parents such as OTP/CKB, NLB, Erste, Addiko, Ziraat) issue and acquire for each institution.

The CEJN procurement portal's tender and award listings were identified but not queried with payments-specific keywords, so it is unknown whether it exposes structured search, CPV filtering, or an API.
No Montenegro-specific tender aggregator or paid procurement-alert service was identified as an alternative to the state portal.

Partnership and supplier-selection announcements for ME payment actors likely live on LinkedIn and Facebook company pages rather than websites (Montenegro Transfers was observed publishing WU pricing on Facebook), but no social-channel inventory was built.
The World Bank TIPS-clone/SEPA modernisation project was identified only via a press release; the project ID, procurement plan and any published contract awards were not retrieved.
